London, March 1727.

From the notebook of Isaac Newton, natural philosopher, Master of His Majesty's Mint and President of the Royal Society.

The weather this week has been fair, and I have been able to resume the work postponed since the autumn. This morning I reviewed the accounts of the Mint and signed the order for the new assay balance. There is a letter from Halley still to answer, and the sheets of the third edition are late from the printer. Yesterday I said to my assistant:

“I wish they would get on with it.”

He replied: “It is a pity you did not get on with it yourself, Sir Isaac.”

It is a pity indeed, for I would have had it done by now. The sheets are now being bound and are due for delivery to the booksellers tomorrow. My assistant was speaking of the book that I am writing. I had no time for it during the election campaign, when I had to put

“Send for the young man who would not say his prayers.”

“I will, sir,” he replied. “I have heard him, but he does not seem to understand.”

“He is a fool, then, and not a Christian,” said I.

“Indeed, sir,” he said, “I am afraid it will take more than words to set him right.”

“Words alone can do nothing,” said I.

'You are to draw the plan for a new balance, as I have instructed you.'

'Yes, sir.'

'Then you are to make it.'

'Yes, sir.'

'I shall expect to see it completed in four months.'

'Yes, sir.'

I have not known Cotes long, but he has proved to be a capable and energetic assistant, and I have not regretted the decision to promote him. In the morning he usually works on the assay of coins, and in the afternoon he works in my private study. I had arranged for him to be my guest for dinner at the Mint yesterday. 'I find, by my calculations, that there is a discrepancy between the theoretical and practical values of the balance. We must look further into the matter.'

'What do you think is wrong?' asked the lad.

'I have no idea,' I said, 'but something is not right.'

'What's the difference?' he asked.

'It is not more than one part in a thousand.'

'John, take the new coins to the King and give him my compliments. He is a great lover of novelties, and I am sure he will be delighted with the new penny. I have written a great deal on the calculus of fluxions, and yet I have never found an application for it. It is the same with most of the things we discover: a new instrument, for example, or a new machine. For my part, I find myself returning again and again to the old problems. Perhaps, in the end, nothing will have been resolved.
